chunks: Temperature control loops in chips and systems. The question: What sort of temperature control loops are commonly implemented?
Chips and systems keep their temperature in check with feedback loops. A sensor measures the temperature. A controller compares it with a limit.
An actuator, such as a fan or a clock-speed reduction, pushes the temperature back down. Several loops run at different speeds, and a hardware trip is the last resort.
Temperature responds slowly, so the loops must be tuned carefully.
Think of a home thermostat with a heater. When the room falls below 19 degrees Celsius, the heater turns on. When it reaches 21 degrees Celsius, the heater turns off.
The two settings stop it from flicking on and off every second. Because the room takes minutes to warm and cool, the temperature always swings gently between the two settings.
A chip's thermal loop behaves the same way. Its actuator reduces speed instead of heating.
The generic thermal loop. Every layer on a real system, on-die throttle, fan control, power cap, is an instance of this shape with a different sensor, actuator and speed.
The plant block is the slow one, and its lag is what makes tuning hard.
Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon, which the limits refer to.
Hysteresis: a different temperature to turn an action on than to turn it off, to prevent rapid flipping. Throttling: reducing speed or power when the chip gets too hot.
PID controller: a controller that reacts to the temperature error, its running total and its rate of change.
Thermal time constant: how many seconds the temperature takes to respond to a change in power. Limit cycle: a steady back-and-forth swing around a threshold.
A chip with theta equals 0. 5 K/W (0. 5 degrees Celsius per watt) sits in 35 degrees Celsius air. At 150 watts, it would settle at 35 plus 150 times 0.
5 equals 110 degrees Celsius, above a 95 degrees Celsius limit. So throttling drops the power to 100 watts, which settles near 85 degrees Celsius.
The loop turns throttling on at 95 degrees Celsius and off at 90 degrees Celsius, so the temperature swings between those marks, about 6 times a minute with a 10 seconds time constant.
That is the whole idea.
"Thermal control is a stack of feedback loops. On-chip sensors drive fast throttling, via DVFS, clock reduction or power caps, often with hysteresis or a stepped governor.
At the system level, a fan controller runs a PWM curve or a PID loop on temperature. Underneath all that is a hardware thermal trip as the last resort.
Because the thermal plant is slow and lagged, the loops have to be tuned so they don't oscillate or overshoot the junction limit."
